source_note: This is an original interactive retelling, not a translation. The myth notes point to the real sources and explain where tellings differ. The young protagonist and the choices are invented for the game.
title: The Sun in the Cave
subtitle: A choose-your-path retelling of Amaterasu and the heavenly rock cave
tagline: The sun is hiding. The kami have a mirror, a string of jewels and a very loud dance. You have two hands.
intro: The sun has hidden in the heavenly rock cave, and the whole world has gone grey. You are a village child with two hands and a loud voice. The kami are gathering on the sky road with a mirror, a string of curved jewels, and a dance that might just work. Choose what you carry. Choose what you shout. Bring the light back.
setting: A rice-farming village below Ama-no-Iwato, the heavenly rock cave

paths.title: The Mirror
paths.blurb: Carry the great mirror up the sky road. Hold it steady at the cave door and let the sun see how bright she is.

paths.title: The Jewels
paths.blurb: String the curved jewels with the patient kami. Every bead is a prayer, and the sun is listening.

paths.title: The Dance
paths.blurb: Drum on Uzume's tub. Keep the beat, learn the joke, and laugh at exactly the right moment.

boons.ownBead: Added a bead of your own
boons.gaveJewels: Gave the jewels to the door

endings.title: A New Dawn
endings.blurb: The mirror does its work. The sun steps out, and a straw rope keeps the light where the world can reach it.

endings.title: The Laughing Sun
endings.blurb: You laugh at exactly the right moment. The cave door bangs open, and the sun comes out giggling.

endings.title: The Light You Keep
endings.blurb: The world gets its sun back. You keep one small, warm coin of it in your pocket.

endings.title: The Long Night
endings.blurb: The laugh stays stuck. The light comes back slowly, and the world learns to keep lamps.

village.title: The Morning Without Sun
village.location: The rice fields below the mountain
village.artCaption: Grey rice fields, a faded torii and no sun in the sky
text: The sun did not come up this morning. You are {name}, standing in the rice field with your hoe still in your hand. The sky is the colour of a wet stone. The roosters have gone quiet.

Your grandmother points at the mountain. 'Amaterasu has hidden in the rock cave,' she says. 'Her brother spoiled her fields and made a dreadful mess in her hall. She is very cross, and she has taken the light with her.'
All night the kami climb the sky road. A kami is a sacred power, a spirit of sun or storm or stone, not a superhero. They carry a great mirror, a string of curved jewels, and a great deal of noise.
A tall kami with kind eyes stops beside you. 'Small one,' she says, 'we need brave helpers. Which will you carry?'

lore.title: Amaterasu and the rock cave
lore.body: Amaterasu is the sun kami of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. When her brother Susanoo wrecked her rice fields and her hall, she withdrew into Ama-no-Iwato, the heavenly rock cave, and the world went dark. 'Kami' means a sacred power or spirit—of sun, storm, mountain or ancestor—not simply a superhero.

choices.label: Take the great mirror and follow the mirror-bearers
Take the string of curved jewels and thread them
Join Uzume and her big empty tub

mirror-1.title: The Mirror on the Sakaki Tree
mirror-1.location: The sky road above the cave
mirror-1.artCaption: A great round mirror hung on a tree beside a rock door
text: The mirror is heavier than it looks. It is a round bronze disc, cool at first, then warm as a fresh bowl of rice. You carry it up the sky road with both arms.
The gods stop at a sakaki tree beside the cave door. They tie the mirror to the branches with white paper streamers. The streamers flutter, though there is no wind.
An old kami shows you where to stand. 'Do not point it at yourself,' he says. 'We need the sun to look, not you.' Then he laughs, because you are already peeking.
Your grandmother's little hand-mirror is in your pocket, next to a rice cake. Behind the cave door, something enormous breathes. The whole mountain is warm, like bread.

lore.title: Yata-no-Kagami, the sacred mirror
lore.body: By tradition the great mirror is Yata-no-Kagami, one of the three regalia of the Japanese imperial line. The Kojiki says the kami hung it on a sakaki tree at the cave mouth. It is now kept at Ise Jingu, the Grand Shrine of Ise, where it is honoured as the dwelling of the sun kami.

choices.label: Hold the mirror steady and watch only the cave door
Polish the bronze with your sleeve until it shines
Ask the mirror politely to do its best

mirror-2.title: The Bright Face in the Door
mirror-2.artCaption: A thin line of gold light along a rock door
text: The cave door is a crack of gold now. Something on the other side is listening. You hear a sleeve rustle and a small, cross sigh.
Uzume shouts a joke. The gods roar. The door opens one hand's width. There she is: a brightness with a face, squinting out at the crowd. She looks tired and furious and wonderful, all at once.
You lift the mirror. She sees herself in it, and stops. Her light fills the sky road, and everyone forgets to breathe.
For one long moment the sun is looking at the sun. The mirror trembles in your hands. Your grandmother's little mirror sits warm against your ribs.

lore.title: She saw her own radiance
lore.body: In the Kojiki, Amaterasu opens the door a crack, and the mirror is held up so that she sees her own radiance. She steps out, astonished. The strong kami Tajikarao pulls the door wide, and a shimenawa, a straw rope, is stretched behind her so she cannot hide again.

choices.label: Hold the mirror high. Call out, 'This is the light the world misses!'
Slip your grandmother's little mirror into your sleeve

jewels-1.title: A String of Curved Jewels
jewels-1.location: The sky road above the cave
jewels-1.artCaption: Curved beads resting on red cloth beside a rock door
text: The jewels arrive in a wooden box lined with red cloth. Each bead is curved like a comma, green or white or dark red. Each one is warm, as if it had been in the sun.
You sit cross-legged and thread them on a cord. A kami with ink-stained fingers shows you the old pattern: three green, one white, two green. The cord smells of cedar.
'Every bead is a prayer someone forgot to say,' she tells you. 'String them, and the prayers come back.' You try very hard not to drop any.
On the roof, the long-crowing roosters of the dawn wake up and practise. Their voices crack. You laugh, and the kami laughs with you.

lore.title: Yasakani-no-Magatama
lore.body: The curved jewels are Yasakani-no-Magatama, the second of the three imperial regalia. Magatama are comma-shaped beads of jade, agate or talc, strung as necklaces in very old Japanese tombs. In the cave story the kami string them on the sacred tree for the sun to see.

choices.label: Thread the beads in the old pattern, exactly
Add one bead of your own at the very end
Ask the roosters to crow at the right moment

jewels-2.title: The Gift at the Cave Door
jewels-2.artCaption: Jewels glowing in the crack of a rock door
text: The cave door slides open a finger's width. Gold light spills out and runs down the mountainside like honey. The gods push the jewel string into your hands and step back.
Nobody says anything. Everybody looks at you. Inside, Amaterasu is humming a small, cross tune. It is the tune your grandmother hums when she is pretending not to be upset.
The jewels catch the light and throw tiny suns across the rock. Your hands are shaking, so you hold them tighter.
Uzume's tub thumps once. The roosters take a breath. Somewhere behind you, a kami whispers, 'Now.' The word travels down the whole crowd like a shiver.

lore.title: Sakaki and shide
lore.body: The tree at the cave mouth is a sakaki, an evergreen used in Shinto ritual. White folded paper, called shide, marks purity and the presence of kami. Cloth and jewels were hung on the branches as offerings. At shrines today you still see sakaki branches with shide beside the gate.

choices.label: Hang the whole string on the door, where she must reach for it
Drape the jewels on Uzume and tell her to dance

dance-1.title: Uzume Turns Over a Tub
dance-1.location: The sky road above the cave
dance-1.artCaption: An upturned tub and a red cord on the rock road
text: Uzume finds you a tub, flips it upside down, and hands you two sticks. 'Hit it like you mean it,' she says. Her hair is tied with a red cord and her sleeves are already dusty.
She climbs onto her own tub and begins. Her feet stamp. Her sleeves fly. She pulls a face so silly that a storm kami snorts into his beard.
You keep the beat. The gods crowd the cave mouth, shoulder to shoulder. The noise rolls up the sky road like thunder with a smile.
Uzume winks at you. 'When I laugh,' she whispers, 'you laugh too. The door is listening.'

lore.title: Ame-no-Uzume's dance
lore.body: Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto is a kami of dawn and mirth. In the Kojiki she turns over a tub, stamps on it, and dances so wildly that the gathered kami roar with laughter. Her descendants, the Sarume clan, were linked to ritual dance at the early court.

choices.label: Drum with both hands and do not stop
Watch the gods' faces and time the beat to their laughter
Sing the song your grandmother sings at harvest

dance-2.title: The Laugh That Opens a Door
dance-2.artCaption: Laughing kami crowded before a rock door
text: Uzume's dance gets faster. Her shadow leaps across the cave wall. The gods drum on their knees, on their shields, on each other. Somebody drops a drum and nobody picks it up.
She does the funniest thing you have ever seen. She lifts one eyebrow, stamps twice, and points at the cave door as if it owes her money.
The whole sky road falls about laughing. The door moves. Just a little. A line of gold appears, thin as a hair.
Your chest hurts from trying not to laugh. Your grandmother always said a serious face is a door too. You have to choose.

lore.title: Why laughter opens the door
lore.body: The myth does not free the sun by force. The kami gather, make noise and laugh. Amaterasu's curiosity—why is everyone happy without me?—draws her to the door. Laughter and curiosity do what force could not. Japanese matsuri, shrine festivals, are often loud as well as solemn.

choices.label: Laugh your loudest laugh, right at the cave door
Cover your mouth. Someone should be serious.

ending-new-dawn.title: A New Dawn
ending-new-dawn.artCaption: Gold light pouring over fields and a small distant cave
text: You hold the mirror high and call out. Your voice is small, but the mountain carries it. 'This is the light the world misses!' Your arms are steady. Your heart is not.
The door swings wide. Amaterasu steps out, and the dark runs away from her like spilled ink. The rice fields turn gold. The roosters forget their song and simply crow.
Strong hands pull the door open the rest of the way. A straw rope, thick as your arm, is stretched across it. The cave can never swallow the light again.
The gods cheer. Uzume falls over laughing. Your grandmother is crying and laughing at once, and the sun is warm on your face.

lore.title: The shimenawa
lore.body: A shimenawa is a twisted straw rope hung at shrine gates to mark sacred space. In the cave story it is stretched behind the sun so that she cannot hide again. Amano-Iwato Shrine in Takachiho, Miyazaki, honours the cave. Ise Jingu honours Amaterasu herself.

ending.title: A New Dawn
ending.summary: You held the mirror steady and called the sun by what she is. She stepped out, the rope went up behind her, and the whole grey world turned gold.

ending-laughing-sun.title: The Laughing Sun
ending-laughing-sun.artCaption: A bright sky above a crowd of cheering kami
text: You laugh. It comes out louder than you meant. Uzume laughs back, and the sky road becomes one enormous, happy noise.
The cave door bangs open. Amaterasu is laughing too, one hand over her mouth. She looks surprised to be enjoying herself. The light jumps out of the cave with her and runs everywhere.
It spills over the fields and the roofs and the river. Somebody's hat blows away. Nobody fetches it. Everybody is too busy laughing.
The sun does not just come back. She comes back giggling, and the whole world is warm and slightly ridiculous. You will remember this on grey days.

lore.title: Kagura
lore.body: Kagura is ritual dance offered at Shinto shrines, often with drums, flutes and masks. Tradition connects it to Uzume's dance at the cave. Some kagura is solemn, but much of it is comic and loud, with audience laughter. Joy is treated as a form of offering.

ending.title: The Laughing Sun
ending.summary: You laughed at exactly the right moment. The door banged open, the sun came out giggling, and the world got its light back with a grin.

ending-light-you-keep.title: The Light You Keep
ending-light-you-keep.artCaption: A small hand mirror on a windowsill at dusk
text: You hold the great mirror steady. Then you slip your grandmother's little hand-mirror out of your pocket and keep it closed in your palm.
Amaterasu steps out. The world goes gold. The dark folds itself up and hides behind the mountain, where it belongs.
Later, when the kami are dancing and the roosters are boasting, you open your hand. The little mirror is warm. There is a coin of sunlight in it, small and steady.
On cloudy days you take it out. It is not the sun. It is only a memory of her, and that is enough to light a room.

lore.title: Mirrors in Shinto
lore.body: In Shinto a mirror can be a shintai, a physical object in which a kami is present. It also shows the viewer their own face, and so is linked with honesty and self-knowledge. The mirror at Ise is kept hidden inside the inner shrine; worshippers see only the buildings and the fence.

ending.title: The Light You Keep
ending.summary: The sun came back and the world was bright. You kept your grandmother's little mirror, and with it one warm coin of daylight for the cloudy days.

ending-long-night.title: The Long Night
ending-long-night.artCaption: A deep blue twilight sky with one small lamp glowing
text: You cover your mouth. The laugh gets stuck in your chest. Uzume's dance slows, and the gods look at you, then at the shut door.
The door stays closed. The gold line on the rock thins and disappears. The sky settles into a long blue twilight, like an evening that cannot finish.
Nobody is hurt. The kami keep trying. Uzume dances every night, a little quieter. You leave a lantern at the cave mouth, a bowl of rice, and a note that says sorry.
One morning, weeks later, the door opens by itself. The light that comes out is pale and careful, and it stays. You do not forget the long night. For a while, you keep a lamp by your bed.

lore.title: The many tellings
lore.body: The story appears in both the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki, and the Nihon Shoki gives several variants. In some tellings the sun returns at once; in others the world waits. Regional Fudoki, ancient gazetteers, also record local sun and cave traditions. The myth is not one fixed script.
lore.source: Kojiki, book 1; Nihon Shoki, book 1; Fudoki

ending.title: The Long Night
ending.summary: You held the laugh in, and the door stayed shut. The light returned slowly, weeks later, and the village learned to keep a lamp burning.
